query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a ductile phase-forming element like Cu to the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy will improve its integrity without sacrificing its caloric response.
generation.conditions: under applied magnetic field, hydrostatic pressure, variable temperature, and compressive loading
generation.predicted_outcome: 15% increase in compressive strength and 20% improvement in thermal conductivity
generation.boundary: operating temperature below 500°C and pressure below 100 MPa
generation.uncertainty: effect of Cu content on phase stability and caloric response

falsification_experiment.design: compression test and thermal conductivity measurement
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: if the alloy with added Cu shows less than 10% increase in compressive strength or less than 15% improvement in thermal conductivity, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: AbstractInvestigation into non-equiatomic high-entropy alloys has grown in recent years due to questions about the role of entropy stabilization in forming single-phase solid solutions. Non-equiatomic alloys have been shown to retain the outstanding mechanical properties exhibited by their equiatomic counterparts and even improve electrical, thermal, and magnetic properties, albeit with relaxed composition bounds. However, much remains to understand the processing–structure–property relationships in all classes of so-called high-entropy alloys (HEAs). Here, we are motivated by the natural phenomena of crystal growth and equilibrium conditions to introduce a method of HEA development where controlled processing conditions determine the most probable and stable composition. This is demonstrated by cooling an equiatomic CrMnFeCoNiCu alloy from the melt steadily over 3 days (cooling rate ~4 °C/h). The result is an alloy containing large Cr-rich precipitates and an almost Cr-free matrix exhibiting compositions within the MnFeCoNiCu system (with trace amounts of Cr).
